NON-GAAP FINANCIAL MEASURES To supplement the consolidated financial statements, which are prepared and presented in accordance with GAAP, we use the following non-GAAP financial measures: Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA Margin, and Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA and Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA Margin. Accordingly, Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA and Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA Margin are not required by, nor presented in accordance with GAAP, but rather are supplemental measures of operating performance of our restaurants. You should be aware that these measures are not indicative of overall results for the Company and that Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA and Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA Margin do not accrue directly to the benefit of stockholders because of corporate-level expenses excluded from such measures. These measures are supplemental measures of operating performance and our calculations thereof may not be comparable to similar measures reported by other companies. These measures are important measures to evaluate the performance and profitability of our restaurants, individually and in the aggregate, but also have important limitations as analytical tools and should not be considered in isolation as substitutes for analysis of our results as reported under GAAP. Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA Margin Adjusted EBITDA represents net income before depreciation and amortization, interest expense, interest income, and income taxes, adjusted for the impact of certain non-cash and other items that we do not consider in our evaluation of ongoing core operating performance as identified in the reconciliation of net income, the most directly comparable GAAP measure to Adjusted EBITDA. Adjusted EBITDA Margin represents Adjusted EBITDA as a percentage of total revenues. We use Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA Margin (i) to evaluate our operating results and the effectiveness of our business strategies, (ii) internally as benchmarks to compare our performance to that of our competitors and (iii) as factors in evaluating management’s performance when determining incentive compensation. We believe that Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA Margin are important measures of operating performance because they eliminate the impact of expenses that do not relate to our core operating performance. We are unable to reconcile the long-term outlook for Adjusted EBITDA to net income, the corresponding U.S. GAAP measure, due to variability and difficulty in making accurate forecasts and projections and because not all information necessary to prepare the reconciliation is available to us without unreasonable efforts. For the same reasons, we are unable to address the probable significance of the unavailable information because we cannot accurately predict all of the components of the adjusted calculations and the non-GAAP measure may be materially different than the GAAP measure. Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA and Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA Margin Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA is defined as revenue, less restaurant operating expenses, which include cost of goods sold (excluding depreciation and amortization), labor expenses, occupancy expenses and other operating expenses. Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA excludes corporate level expenses and depreciation and amortization on restaurant property and equipment. Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA Margin represents Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA as a percentage of revenue. We believe that Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA and Restaurant-Level Adjusted EBITDA Margin are important measures to evaluate the performance and profitability of our restaurants, individually and in the aggregate. title: Against All Oddities: Tractor Tales
summary: The crew and I at our ex-foundry-now-car-commune have amassed a sizable collection of not-so-sizable tractors and mowers. There’s always work to be done around the shop, farm, and garden, and somewhere among the fleet is a tractor ready to work if you look hard enough. (Except last week, when circumstances demanded I buy an electric […]
body_text: The crew and I at our ex-foundry-now-car-commune have amassed a sizable collection of not-so-sizable tractors and mowers. There’s always work to be done around the shop, farm, and garden, and somewhere among the fleet is a tractor ready to work if you look hard enough. (Except last week, when circumstances demanded I buy an electric mower.) To my great fortune, I have been viewed as a custodian of junk, so people just give me these things for free. No cost up front, but a lot down the line. Still, a free tractor is a free tractor. So what projects and associated headaches have we managed to collect so far? Matthew Anderson The first is a 1968 Bolens 1225 that my wife inherited from her late grandfather. It was maintained meticulously, even down to the switchgear descriptions printed on a label maker. From the afterlife, I know he must have cringed when I fabbed up a ridiculously loud stack for it, but he likely smiled when I used it to drive through our neighborhood in Charleston to go pick up tacos. Rumor has it that there is even security footage of my wife sitting on my lap as we brap-brap-brapped down Poplar Street at 2 a.m. on New Year’s Day. After we moved to Germany, the Bolens floated from a friend’s shop in Savannah, to a shop in Durham, and finally to a spot underneath my buddy’s porch. (The same friend who had a certain Century sitting back there.) A couple years back, the Bolens returned home and has been sitting, photogenically, in the shop. Doing nothing and asking for nothing. I believe it was called upon once to clear ice from the driveway, but its turf tires and unweighted rear wheels just bunny hopped. It was so embarrassing that I just parked it. Wheel weights and real tractor tires would be nice! The first Wheel Horse tractor that I ever got was a 20-hp Onan V-twin-powered 520-H model that was donated by Shade Tree Garage around the same time I started relocating cars out to my home in Statesville. I had thrown it in the back of my father’s truck along with a vintage armoire and was towing a Holden Commodore behind it. It was quite the hillbilly setup, which is kind of our style, if you’re new around here. That mower started on the key right off the rip and served beautifully, with little more attention than biweekly air in the right rear tire. Studebakers and Red Tractors. Matthew Anderson Until recently, that is. For some reason, multiple issues have befallen the old red steed. It took quite a bit of diagnosing in the back barn at the house, but I ultimately identified an intermittently faulty starter relay, a burned-up battery cable, a questionable battery, and the real heart of the issue: a blown fuse… probably caused by the untrustworthy battery cable. As with most electrical troubleshooting, I eventually found three unrelated problems and one actual problem. This forensic work happened at night, in fits and starts throughout the course of a week. All the while, I was trying to keep up with summer grass growth using the gifted Honda push mower that I had previously killed (bent crank) hitting half-buried slag chunks at the foundry. I dubbed it Olde Wobbly. After several nights of working outside, supervised by a family of skunks and actively interrogated by raccoons, none of whom offered a useful diagnosis, I was finally able to permanently retire Olde Wobbly back to the foundry interior. This was not expected. Matthew Anderson Work at my house continued. My friend Johna-fun volunteered to help us rip out our old overgrown fence line and go on an invasive plant massacre with his three-cylinder Kubota. Pretty amazing how much work you can get done with a tractor when it actually starts every time. Between Johna-fun and his son (our foundry intern), they’ve done an immense amount of ground clearing at the foundry and at home. Inspiration! Longtime readers likely remember the International 504 on which I had bushhogged as a teen. Again, Shadetree Garage (and dairy farm owner) Truett entrusted me with the tractor. Nowadays, I regularly commute between home and shop on this old beast. Eventually, the road miles took their toll, bringing a large power steering leak and a generator so noisy that it was starting to drown out the clattery diesel engine. Deciding I had enough vehicles to cross-reference parts to and from, I caved and just brought the generator by Phil’s Starter & Alternator along with the smoked alternator from the Hobby 600. While that was down for rebuild, I was able to locate the leaking power steering line, and all it took was a light cinch to get it back in working order. Now, with a functioning charging system and steering that goes where I point it without a steady stream of oil accompanying the request—a true luxury, in this economy—it was time for some real work. Some months ago, I had found a really nice boom pole that I painted in the proper International red. Time to put it to the test. The old smelter unit from the foundry was buried deep in the brush, and we were gonna pull it out. With questionable rigging, head foundry gremlin Thomas was able to yank the thing out of the blackberry and maypop vines so it could be moved up to the driveway for use as a planter and part of a drainage system. Somewhere in all this, one of the calcium carbonate-filled rear tires suffered a puncture, and now I’m looking at a pair of new rear tires. Honestly, the 504 deserves some pampering. Cha-ching! Thomas preparing to hurt himself. Matthew Anderson The fourth tractor I’m about to mention was my actual first: the 1971 single-cylinder Wheel Horse pictured below. I first took the wheel of this thing when I was around 12 years old. At that point, it had been fitted with agricultural tires, wheel weights, and the mower deck was removed. To 12-year-old me, this was less of a tractor and more of a pickup truck saddled with dramatically lower expectations. I had a trailer made from a Whippet axle and some barn wood bonking around behind me at all times, usually equipped with some tools, PB Blaster, and starter fluid to kill the wasps. I was many times entrusted to drive down Carpenter Pond Road to go retrieve things from Truett’s son’s house, a feat one would not dare do today, mainly because there are a lot more people around to whine about a kid towing a trailer full of chemicals. Nearly every day I would drive deep down into the woods in search of Studebaker parts or just to be among the old Packards, Citroens, and a myriad of other weird vintage European cars. Back to modern times. When Truett came by the foundry to pick up his son’s 1941 Studebaker we had been working on, he brought with him my old tractor, strapped down on the inbound trailer, as payment. I couldn’t believe my eyes. What a treat to have my first real taste of freedom back at my fingertips. The same old agricultural tires from the 1990s are still on it, and they’re entirely in need of replacement. I dropped everything to focus on this valuable piece of junk. I have thrown a new battery in it and verified that it gets fuel, just no spark. We suspect that it won’t take much more than filing the points to get it manually shifting back through the gears again. I can feel a spendy repair coming, and I don’t care. Wheel Horse in optimal configuration. Matthew Anderson I should mention that my old rig wasn’t alone on Truett’s Trailer of Tetanusy Gifts. There was another larger two-cylinder Wheel Horse included, the one that I used to mow the lawn with back in the day, again out at the garage/farm. This sort of utility is becoming increasingly necessary as the foundry has developed an appetite for push mowers that borders on irresponsible. (First Olde Wobbly, then another one I had stashed away in storage.) The bent blades, broken cranks, carbs full of schmoo, and hours-long mow times were adding up. My zero-down plus battery, fuel pump, battery-cable installment plan for the old mower was crucial. Now it runs beautifully, perhaps even on a fraction of the gas I last used to cut the grass 25 years ago. Foundry security footage now certainly exists of me smiling like an idiot while doing lawn maintenance. Well, my wife’s Bolens continues to look pretty in the shop, we have two 520-H “Red Square” Wheel Horses cutting grass, three running push mowers, a charging-and-not leaking 504 with a tire that holds air (for now), and I haven’t even been sprayed by a skunk. Let’s ride this momentum, people! Gotta start somewhere. Matthew Anderson Buddy, you know that thing’s not going to do jack without field current. Matthew Anderson Studebakers and Red Tractors, just like back at Shadetree Matthew Anderson Look what the cat dragged in. Matthew Anderson Family affair. Matthew Anderson Motorsport electronics by day… Matthew Anderson Johna-fun and Jonas on the running tractor. Matthew Anderson The two most attractive ones. Matthew Anderson Studebakers and Red Tractors, just like back at Shadetree Matthew Anderson Next job – yank the motor out of the Beta. Matthew Anderson Some gave all. Matthew Anderson Matthew Anderson Matthew Anderson The post Against All Oddities: Tractor Tales appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: Is Pharmacy Delivery Driving Loyalty or Draining Your Margin?
summary: Pharmacy delivery can build loyalty, but it also creates hidden costs. Learn how independent pharmacies can evaluate delivery ROI and build a more sustainable model.
body_text: Pharmacy delivery can be a loyalty engine or a margin leak. For patients, delivery can make medication access easier when transportation, work, mobility, or caregiving responsibilities make pharmacy visits difficult. For independent pharmacies, it can strengthen patient relationships. ‍ However, delivery does not automatically create a return just because patients want it. The real question is whether the pharmacy has a manageable model for coordinating routes, collecting payment, communicating with patients, and completing deliveries. ‍ A small delivery program may be easy to manage. As demand grows, driver time, routing complexity, and staff coordination can increase quickly. ‍ Delivery is becoming a competitive expectation ‍ Convenience matters to patients. But offering free or same-day delivery without clear boundaries can create hidden costs. ‍ Before expanding, ask how many patients are requesting delivery, how many stops your team can complete, and how much staff time goes into each one. The answers can point to a need for delivery windows, route days, geographic limits, or fees. ‍ What belongs in a delivery ROI review? ‍ The cost of delivery includes more than the driver or courier. Review the full workflow, including: Driver or courier costs Mileage and fuel Staff time spent coordinating deliveries Payment collection and follow-up Missed or rescheduled deliveries Completed prescriptions Patient retention and refill activity ‍ A delivery program may look affordable when you only count the cost of the route. The return can look different when you account for the time your team spends confirming details, answering status questions, collecting payment, and resolving missed deliveries. ‍ The value side matters, too. Delivery may help complete prescriptions that would otherwise remain unclaimed, reduce routine follow-up for staff, and give patients another reason to return to the pharmacy. ‍ The delivery volume trap ‍ Many pharmacies start delivery for a small group of patients, but as more people request it, the program may require a different operating model. ‍ A pharmacy that manages a few deliveries between other tasks may struggle when routes grow. Payment follow-up and status questions can also increase with volume. ‍ The goal is to create a model that can grow without adding the same amount of manual work each time. ‍ Guardrails that protect delivery ROI Common delivery guardrails include: Batching deliveries Offering delivery on defined days or within specific windows Setting a geographic service area Charging a delivery fee or defining a number of free deliveries Collecting digital payment before fulfillment when appropriate Sending automated prescription and delivery updates These policies make delivery more predictable for patients and easier for staff to manage. They also help the pharmacy understand what it can offer consistently. Operating delivery efficiently ‍ A delivery capability gets medication from the pharmacy to the patient, and the workflow around the delivery determines how much work the pharmacy absorbs. ‍ Patients need to know when a prescription is ready, what they owe, when delivery is expected, and what happens next. When notifications, payment, delivery status, and refill reminders are handled as separate manual tasks, the experience can feel fragmented and the work can add up quickly. ‍ A more connected experience can reduce friction for patients while limiting repetitive follow-up for the pharmacy team. ‍ How NimbleRx fits alongside the pharmacy workflow ‍ NimbleRx works alongside a pharmacy’s existing workflow to connect prescription-ready notifications, digital checkout, applicable signature or approval steps, fulfillment coordination, secure communication, and refill engagement. ‍ The goal is to connect the patient-facing steps around delivery, from prescription ready through checkout, fulfillment, and the next refill. That can reduce uncertainty for patients and manual follow-up for staff. ‍ Start with a simple delivery audit ‍ Review one month of delivery activity and ask: How many deliveries did we complete? What did each one truly cost, including staff time? How many required payment or status follow-up? Where did patients get stuck? What helped patients return for their next refill? ‍ Better delivery ROI does not mean making every delivery free. It means building a delivery model that patients value and your pharmacy can sustain. ‍ Talk to our team to see how NimbleRx can connect patient communications, digital checkout, and fulfillment with your existing pharmacy workflow. ‍

title: ​Pediatrician's Guide: 5 Simple Steps to Treat Your Child's Dry Skin and Winter Eczema
summary: When cold weather hits, many parents find themselves battling rough, itchy patches on their child's skin. The shift in season—low humidity outdoors combined with indoor heating—strips moisture from the skin and can lead to dry winter skin or cause eczema (also known as atopic dermatitis) to flare.
body_text: When cold weather hits, many parents find themselves battling rough, itchy patches on their child's skin. The shift in season—low humidity outdoors combined with indoor heating—strips moisture from the skin and can lead to dry winter skin or cause eczema (also known as atopic dermatitis) to flare. ‍ As a parent, your main focus during the winter months should be restoring and protecting your child’s delicate skin barrier, which acts like a protective shield. The good news is that most winter skin issues, including mild baby eczema, can be managed or prevented with a few simple, consistent changes to your daily routine. ‍ The most effective pediatrician-recommended strategy is to avoid irritating triggers, restore the skin barrier using thick, occlusive moisturizers, and in some cases use topical medications to help clear up the skin. ‍ Why Is My Child's Skin So Vulnerable to Winter Dryness? Winter dryness happens primarily because low humidity, both outside and inside your home, actively pulls water directly out of the skin. This rapid moisture loss occurs because cold, dry air causes the skin's outer layer to thin as water evaporates out. Low Indoor Humidity: During Winter, as more time is spent indoors where the humidity is lower, water evaporates from your child’s skin at an accelerated rate. Worse for Eczema: For children who already have a diagnosis of eczema, this intense dryness creates microscopic cracks in the skin barrier. This allows irritants like harsh soaps or dust mites to enter more easily, quickly triggering inflammation and uncomfortable winter eczema flare ups. This also thins the immune layer of the skin, increasing the risk of both bacterial and viral skin infections. ‍ Choosing the Right Defense: Best Moisturizer for Baby Eczema in Winter Moisturizing is an important step for treating dry skin during winter, but the type of product you use and when you apply it are critical factors. You should aim to apply moisturizer liberally at least twice a day, especially immediately after bathing. It’s important to make sure that all products applied to the skin are fragrance free, unexpired, and hypoallergenic. ‍ 1. Choose the Right Moisturizer During the cold months, you need thicker products to create a durable protective barrier against the harsh, dry air. Ointments (Best for skin protection): These are the thickest products, like Vaseline or Aquafor , that form a protective barrier that sits on top of the skin, rather than being absorbed, to physically block water loss. They are superior to creams or lotions for tackling severe winter dryness. Creams (Best for daily skin hydration): Thicker than standard lotions, creams contain high occlusive and emollient content to restore the lipid barrier and smooth the skin. Look for ingredients like ceramides, cholesterol, or shea butter. Avoid Lotions: Lotions contain more water and less oil, which makes them less effective at creating the durable, protective barrier needed in dry winter conditions. ‍ 2. Master the "Soak and Seal" Method The goal of this pediatrician-recommended method is to trap the hydration your child's skin absorbs during the bath before it evaporates into the dry air. Soak. Give a brief bath (5–10 minutes maximum) using lukewarm— not hot—water. Use a small amount of gentle baby soap, or even just plain water. Pat Dry. Gently pat the skin with a soft towel, ensuring it remains slightly damp. Avoid rubbing the skin, which can irritate an already compromised barrier. Seal. Immediately apply the thick cream or ointment. The optimal time to apply the moisturizer is within three minutes of exiting the water, effectively locking in the moisture. ‍ How Should I Change My Child's Bathing and Cleansing Routine? Your child’s bath routine should always support their skin barrier, not strip it of natural protection. Lukewarm Water is Key: Hot water feels comfortable, but it strips away the skin’s natural surface lipids, which leads to a major increase in dryness after cleansing. Always keep the water temperature lukewarm. Choose Mild Cleansers: For children and babies prone to winter eczema , avoid traditional bar soaps, bubble baths, and soaps that are highly alkaline or fragranced. Instead, opt for oil-based cleansers that minimally disrupt the lipid barrier. Pediatricians highly recommend fragrance-free products for all sensitive and eczema-prone babies and children. ‍ Environmental Changes to Prevent Dryness Since the cold, dry air is the main trigger for dry skin in winter, controlling your indoor environment is crucial for kid's dry skin during winter. Use a Humidifier: Running a cool-mist humidifier in your child's bedroom and main living areas can help maintain an optimal humidity level, somewhere around 40% max. This physically reduces the rate of water evaporation from their skin. Remember to clean the humidifier frequently to prevent mold growth, which can also be a significant eczema trigger. Dress in Soft Layers: Avoid putting rough materials like wool or abrasive synthetic fabrics directly against your child’s skin, as this can cause mechanical irritation. Choose soft cotton or breathable synthetic fabrics as a comfortable base layer. Layering is important because it prevents overheating and sweating, which can also trigger eczema flares. Gentle Laundry: Use fragrance-free and dye-free laundry detergents. Skip fabric softeners or dryer sheets, which can leave irritating residues that bother sensitive skin. If you are concerned about persistent itching or reactions, review common household allergens for kids. ‍ Urgent Check: When to Call Your Pediatrician for a Rash or Skin Infection While basic, consistent skin care can help dry skin, eczema is a chronic, inflammatory condition that often requires medical intervention during a severe winter flare. If you are following the recommended steps and not seeing improvement, it's time to seek professional advice. ‍ Contact your pediatrician immediately for a virtual visit if you notice any of the following signs: Persistent Itching: The itchiness is intense, persistent, or is actively keeping your child awake at night, even with regular use of frequent moisturizers and ointments. Worsening Rash: The rash does not improve after one week of diligent moisturizing and routine adjustments. Signs of Infection: The skin becomes painful, hot, swollen, or develops open sores, blisters, crusting, or yellow/honey-colored weeping. These symptoms may indicate an infection requiring antibiotics or prescription treatment. ‍ Your pediatrician may recommend targeted therapeutic strategies to address a severe flare: Topical Steroids: These are often the first line of defense to quickly reduce acute inflammation and associated itching during a flare. Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors (TCIs): These are non-steroidal alternatives sometimes used for maintenance therapy on sensitive areas, preventing future flares without the risks associated with long-term steroid use. Your child’s PCP or dermatologist would decide if this is appropriate as it is a long-term treatment option. Wet Wrap Therapy (WWT): For severe, widespread flares, WWT involves applying moisturizer and medication, then covering the area with a damp layer of cloth followed by a dry layer to enhance hydration and medication absorption. ‍ Key Takeaways for Winter Skin Care Seal Moisture Immediately: Always use thick creams or ointments within three minutes of a lukewarm bath (the pediatrician-recommended "soak and seal" method). Control the Air: Keep indoor humidity around 40% using a clean humidifier to combat low winter moisture. Protect the Barrier: Avoid hot water, harsh soaps, and rough fabrics that can irritate sensitive skin. Know When to Call: If dryness or eczema is painful, red, infected, or prevents your child from sleeping, seek pediatric care right away. If you are concerned about persistent dry skin, eczema, or need prescription treatment for a flare-up, you can speak with one of our pediatric experts without an appointment, 24/7.​

title: Online Reputation Management Is Built One Response at a Time
summary: Use online reputation management to monitor brand mentions, respond to customer reviews professionally, strengthen credibility, and earn customer trust.
body_text: A reputation is the pattern people see across reviews, search results, social posts, news mentions, and the company website. Online reputation management helps a team notice those signals, decide what deserves action, and respond without making a difficult moment worse. The work has four connected parts. Monitoring brand mentions consistently helps a business see conversations early. Responding to customer reviews professionally shows how the business behaves under attention. Building positive online credibility gives people reliable evidence beyond a single comment, while improving customer trust online depends on matching public promises with what customers actually experience. Read the signal before reacting to the emotion Strikingly Online Review Monitoring brand mentions consistently starts with verification. Save the link, date, platform, claim, and any order or support details the team can check. An angry comment may identify a real service failure, while a calm one may contain a factual error. Separate tone from substance before judging the mention. Monitoring brand mentions consistently goes beyond tagged social posts. Track the business name, misspellings, product names, spokesperson names, and campaign phrases across review sites, search, social platforms, and relevant publications. Strikingly's guide to online brand monitoring recommends alerts and sentiment review instead of waiting for an issue to become obvious. Record five facts before choosing a response Accuracy: What can the team verify, and what remains an allegation? Impact: Is this one person's complaint or evidence of a repeated failure? Reach: Who is likely to see the mention, now and through search later? Risk: Does it involve safety, privacy, discrimination, fraud, or legal claims? Owner: Who can investigate, approve a remedy, and publish the response? This record turns monitoring brand mentions consistently into repeatable work. It gives online reputation management a fair standard: respond according to evidence and risk, not praise or anger. Building positive online credibility and improving customer trust online both begin with consistent treatment. Online reputation management needs more than one response lane When the criticism is accurate Acknowledge the failure, apologize without excuses, explain the immediate remedy, and state what will prevent a repeat. Responding to customer reviews professionally does not require private details; it requires enough public accountability for a future reader to see that the concern was taken seriously. When the facts are incomplete or disputed Responding to customer reviews professionally in a disputed case means correcting only what can be demonstrated, using neutral language, and inviting the reviewer to compare records privately. Online reputation management should not become a public cross-examination. Building positive online credibility requires separating evidence from assumptions without calling a customer dishonest. When the review is positive Thank the customer and mention one detail so the response does not look automated. Responding to customer reviews professionally includes positive comments because acknowledgment strengthens the relationship without becoming another sales pitch. The Strikingly article on the best ways to respond to reviews likewise emphasizes addressing the points a reviewer raised. When the mention involves serious risk Preserve evidence and escalate safety, privacy, legal, or discrimination claims before writing. A short acknowledgment may be suitable during review. Monitoring brand mentions consistently helps these cases reach the right owner quickly, but speed cannot override accuracy or confidentiality. Online reputation management must serve silent readers too Strikingly's Customer Support with Feedback The reviewer is not the only audience. Potential customers may find the exchange months later, so responding to customer reviews professionally should reveal the business's character. Recognize the concern, address its substance, describe the next action, and provide a suitable contact route. Avoid "sorry you feel that way," which transfers responsibility to the customer. Do not promise an outcome before the facts are known. Explain who will review the concern, what information is needed, and when contact will follow. Responding to customer reviews professionally means making promises the team can keep. That restraint supports improving customer trust online better than an immediate offer that is never completed. Check the reply before publishing Does it acknowledge the customer's actual point rather than repeat a template? Does it avoid private information, blame, sarcasm, and unsupported claims? Does it name a realistic action, owner, or response time? Would the wording still look responsible to someone finding it through search? Has the operational team confirmed that the promised next step can happen? Online reputation management needs one recognizable voice with enough flexibility to sound human. Building positive online credibility depends on consistent values, not identical sentences. Responding to customer reviews professionally therefore requires patience and judgment rather than copy-and-paste apologies. Protect private details while improving customer trust online HiNails Template from Strikingly A public reply should not request account numbers, medical details, addresses, or payment information. Invite the customer to a secure channel and explain how to identify the case. A Strikingly contact form can collect a focused message, while Live Chat provides a direct route for eligible sites. Improving customer trust online still requires public acknowledgment of responsibility. Keep the conversation history with the customer record. Strikingly's guidance for managing contacts and sending one-to-one emails supports continuity. Online reputation management fails when a customer repeats the problem to three people. Give one owner authority to coordinate the answer and update the public thread after resolution. Ask whether the remedy worked, document the result, and update the public response when appropriate. Responding to customer reviews professionally includes this follow-through. It shows that private contact was not a tactic to move criticism out of sight, which is central to improving customer trust online. Building positive online credibility through proof and visible improvement Strikingly Product Review Feature Building positive online credibility is not the same as publishing only praise. Show current business details, clear policies, named expertise, representative testimonials, and changes made after feedback. Strikingly's guide to reputation building connects testimonials, useful content, and prompt responses with stronger trust. For an online store, the Product Reviews feature can request reviews after fulfilled orders and manage which submissions appear. Moderate for relevance, privacy, spam, and prohibited content, not to erase every criticism. Building positive online credibility and improving customer trust online become fragile when the published record looks unrealistically perfect. Look for repeated themes instead of defending each incident separately. If customers mention confusing delivery terms, rewrite the policy and checkout explanation. If support delays recur, change staffing or response expectations. Online reputation management gains value when it repairs the experience behind the reputation. Improving customer trust online then comes from visible change, not polished wording. Responding to customer reviews professionally and publishing proof where it helps a decision are complementary. A service page can show a relevant client outcome; a product page can show verified feedback; an about page can show credentials and press references. Building positive online credibility works when evidence is specific, current, and close to the claim it supports. Ask for reviews at a fair moment and give every customer the same opportunity. The Strikingly guide to encouraging online customer reviews discusses clear requests and accessible review paths. Do not offer rewards that depend on a positive rating. Improving customer trust online requires authentic feedback, not a score shaped by selective pressure. Make monitoring brand mentions consistently sustainable Monitoring brand mentions consistently needs clear coverage and ownership. High-volume businesses may check priority channels throughout the day; a small local business may review alerts and platforms each morning. Define who watches, who can answer, and which risks require escalation. Include untagged mentions and search results, not only notifications delivered by a platform. Create a weekly summary of new mentions, sentiment themes, unanswered reviews, response times, and recurring causes. Monitoring brand mentions consistently is useful when the summary leads to a decision. It may reveal a documentation gap, a product defect, an employee training need, or a positive story worth asking permission to share. Avoid reducing every discussion to a positive-versus-negative score. Monitoring brand mentions consistently can expose rumors or outdated information. Use the website as the stable source of truth, update the relevant page, then link to it from an appropriate response. A Strikingly blog can hold substantial explanations, while clear page titles and descriptions help accurate information appear with context in search. Building positive online credibility requires reliable information the business controls. Measure outcomes that reflect behavior: time to acknowledge, time to resolve, repeated complaint rate, review response coverage, branded search quality, and whether corrected customers return. Built-in Analytics can show how people reach and use supporting pages. Online reputation management should connect those patterns with service records instead of claiming that web traffic alone proves trust. In online reputation management, a thirty-minute weekly review is enough to begin. Select the most important unresolved mention, verify the facts, assign the remedy, and check whether a website page needs correction. Monitoring brand mentions consistently supplies the evidence. Responding to customer reviews professionally makes accountability visible. Building positive online credibility turns resolved issues and real outcomes into useful proof, while improving customer trust online follows when the experience supports the words. Strong online reputation management is not control over what everyone says. It is a dependable practice of listening, answering, fixing, and documenting. Keep the response specific, protect private information, and let repeated feedback change the business. Improving customer trust online becomes a result of responsible conduct rather than a slogan attached to the next campaign.
